units.text: Start with the left panel: meaningful parameter paths organize configuration, while version selection determines which stored value the application requests.
Follow the middle parent folder to its descendants: recursive reads can expose child parameters, so granting a broad parent path can defeat intended child isolation.
On the right, SecureString adds KMS decryption authorization, while application caching can keep an older configuration value in use after the parameter changes.
Return to the whole slide and test the application's actual path, version, decryption permissions and cache behavior before treating its configuration boundary as secure.
The left panel compares storage tiers: Advanced supports larger values, higher parameter counts, policies and supported sharing, while API throughput remains a separate setting.
In the upper-right panel, expiration removes a parameter, while expiration and no-change notifications signal conditions that your own response workflow must handle.
The lower-right panel shows a one-way tier upgrade: an Advanced parameter cannot be downgraded in place, so retain required values before planning recreation.
Read the full comparison as three separate decisions: storage attributes, notification or expiration policy, and the explicit workflow that updates or rotates a credential.
Follow the left diagram from the template to Secrets Manager: a dynamic reference supplies a secret value without placing the plaintext credential directly in the template.
The upper-right panel separates secret changes from deployment: changing only the secret value does not refresh a CloudFormation resource property containing a dynamic reference.
The lower-right panel adds consumer refresh: existing environment variables, connections and application caches may retain old values until the appropriate refresh or restart occurs.
With the full slide visible, verify three operations separately: deployment resolves the reference, the rotation workflow updates credentials, and consumers obtain the current value.
Start with the consuming principal on the left: its identity policy must allow the intended Secrets Manager read for the correct secret and request context.
The middle gate belongs to the secret owner: a resource policy must authorize the external principal, with narrowly scoped permissions and appropriate conditions.
The right gate protects the encryption key: cross-account secret access needs a customer-managed KMS key and the consumer's required decryption permissions in applicable policies.
Read all three gates together and test the real caller: permission to read a secret does not by itself authorize the KMS key used to decrypt it.
